Issued at 326 AM CDT Sat Sep 12 2026

     TODAY THROUGH MONDAY

Bottom line up front: the forecast over the next 24 hours remains 
quite challenging. As of 3AM this morning, a cold front was 
sagging across southern Nebraska with a broken line of 
thunderstorms moving south along with it. Currently, storms are 
only over portions of southeast Nebraska; however, there is some
evidence that continued maintenance of this cluster of storms 
is likely to occur as storms move south across eastern Kansas 
this morning. A subtle mid/upper wave is slowly trekking 
eastward over the High Plains providing marginal upper level 
support for broad ascent. Additionally, the LLJ and subsequent 
moisture transport is nosing into north-central Kansas providing
another subtle source of ascent. An elevated instability 
gradient resides across eastern Kansas, and it's likely storms 
will continue to be focused along this gradient as the cold 
front pushes southward this morning. The biggest challenges with
the morning convection will be, a) the intensity of the storms 
as they push southward across eastern Kansas, and b) how this 
activity will impact storm chances this afternoon and evening. 
At the moment, it appears as though storms across eastern Kansas
this morning will remain sub-severe, but a rouge wind gust up 
to 60 mph or hail stone up to quarter size cannot be ruled out.

Like mentioned previously, the evolution of this morning's activity 
will likely have a major impact on which locations see the 
potential for strong to severe scattered thunderstorms this 
afternoon. It's likely this morning's activity pushes the cold 
front/outflow boundary further south than previously forecasted.
Generally speaking, short term guidance suggests the front will
be stalled out across southern Kansas or northern Oklahoma this
afternoon. SBCAPE along the boundary will be in the 
neighborhood of 2000-2500 J/kg with effective shear around 40 
knots. With this environment, any storm that develops will have 
the opportunity to become strong or severe with up to golfball 
size hail and up to 60 mph wind gusts possible. Confidence is
high storms will develop along the frontal boundary this 
afternoon, especially given surface convergence and strong 
diurnal heating. However, confidence is low on the exact
location of the boundary when CI occurs this afternoon. Later 
this evening into tonight, the LLJ is forecast to ramp up again.
With the mid-level baroclinic zone bisecting the CWA, ample 
mid-level WAA is likely to overspread the area leading to the
development of scattered elevated showers and storms. Again, 
the confidence additional storms will develop tonight is high, 
but the exact location remains in question as short term 
guidance places this activity somewhere between southern Kansas
and southeast Nebraska. Regardless, storm chances will come to 
an end throughout the morning hours on Sunday.

With the aforementioned frontal boundary forecast to wash out by 
Sunday morning, a hot airmass will return to the region by Sunday 
afternoon with highs well into the mid to upper 90s across most of 
the forecast area. Monday is forecast to be potentially hotter with 
some locations possibly reaching 100 Monday afternoon. With 
dewpoints in the mid 60s to low 70s, heat indices exceeding 100 
appears likely each afternoon and evening Sunday and Monday. Monday 
evening into Monday night, another frontal boundary is expected to 
sag into portions of northern and central Kansas. This will be the 
focus for another round of showers and storms Monday night into 
early Tuesday morning across mainly central Kansas.

     TUESDAY THROUGH FRIDAY

Only minimal changes in the forecast have been noted for next week. 
As mentioned in previous forecasts, a strong deep layer trough is 
forecast to traverse into the central/northern plains by Monday, and 
will be the catalyst for the aforementioned cold front sagging into 
Kansas by Monday night. Mid-range guidance continues to suggest the 
frontal boundary will be draped across Kansas from northeast to 
southwest through much of next week. Several perturbations embedded 
within zonal flow aloft will provide the lift necessary for 
potentially several rounds of showers and storms next week. It 
remains way too early to estimate how much rainfall will fall across 
the area, but it appears a number of locations will at least see 
some beneficial rainfall Tuesday through Friday of next week. 
Additionally, some adjustments have been made to the temperature 
forecast. Most notably, afternoon highs across southern and eastern 
Kansas have been raised on Tuesday as compressional warming ahead of 
the front is likely to drive temperatures into the mid to upper 90s,
